lesson.menu_title: Asking Nicely -- and Who You Are Asking
lesson.menu_desc: The same question is perfectly normal in Oslo and a little rude in London. Tonight, indirect questions, and how to choose the right amount of politeness for the person in front of you
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 14 -- Asking Nicely -- and Who You Are Asking
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi | Lesson 14 -- Asking Nicely -- and Who You Are Asking

listenings.text: My name is Eirik, and I am from Bergen, on the west coast of Norway. When I moved to Manchester for my master's degree, I shared a house with an English guy called Tom. In my second week, he said to me, I was just wondering if you might possibly be able to do the dishes at some point. I said, no thank you, I am busy tonight. For me, that was an honest answer to a question. He was asking if I was able to, and I was not. Tom did not speak to me for two days. Later a friend explained that it was not a question at all. It was a request, and quite an urgent one. In Norway we would just say, can you do the dishes, and nobody would find that rude. Now I have learned to listen for the words wondering and possibly. When I hear them, I know that something important is coming.

I am Harriet, I am from Leeds, and three years ago I moved to Oslo with my husband. On my first morning I went to a small café near our flat. The man in front of me said, one coffee, black. No please, no thank you, no smile. I was quite shocked, to be honest. I thought, how rude. Then the woman behind the counter smiled at him and said, of course, and they chatted about the weather for a minute. Nobody was offended except me. When it was my turn, I said, hello, sorry, I was wondering if I could possibly have a coffee, if it is not too much trouble. She looked at me as if I had asked for something very complicated. Now, three years later, I order my coffee in five words. But when I go home to Leeds, I have to remember to put all the sorries back in.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: Polite and respectful, especially to strangers
To give other people a certain impression
Careful not to upset people when you say something difficult
Trying too hard to make somebody do what you want
Uncomfortable, and not sure what to say or do
To give somebody extra work or trouble with a request
Saying exactly what you think, without being gentle
Honest and clear, with no hidden meaning

vocab.text: Look at how many of these words describe the SAME behavior from different sides: blunt and straightforward can describe the same sentence. Which word you choose depends on whether you liked it. The same is true of tactful and beating around the bush.

items.situation: You are in London and you need to find a pharmacy. Ask a stranger.
tips: Sorry, could you tell me where the nearest pharmacy is?
Sorry + could you tell me + statement order.

items.situation: In Oslo, you want to know the price of a sandwich. Ask the Norwegian way.
tips: Direct is fine in Norway. Too much hedging sounds strange.

items.situation: You want to know if the museum is open on Mondays. Ask politely.
tips: Do you know if the museum is open on Mondays?
A yes/no question inside: if or whether.

items.situation: You need your British host to turn down the music. Ask without sounding pushy.
tips: I was wondering if you could turn the music down a little.
I was wondering if + could: very polite, very British.

items.situation: On a train, ask the person next to you to move their bag.
tips: Would you mind moving your bag, please?
Would you mind + -ing. If the answer is no, it means yes.

items.situation: An American friend says: just ask, do not beat around the bush. Ask for a ride to the airport.
tips: Could you give me a ride to the airport on Friday?
Could you is enough. No need for I was wondering here.

answerkey.title: Reveal the answer key
key: Direct: Where is the station? Verb before subject. Normal in Norway and with friends.
Polite: Could you tell me where the station is? The second half has statement order.
No do in the second half: Do you know what time the shop opens? · never what time does the shop open.
Yes/no inside: Do you know if / whether the kitchen closes at nine?
Would you mind + -ing: Would you mind opening the window? No means yes, I will.
Very polite: I was wondering if you could... The past makes it softer.
The more you impose, the more polite you go. A coffee is not a favor.
And the one that is not grammar: Norway is direct, the UK hedges, the US is in the middle. Choose the level for the listener, not for yourself.

reading.rtitle: How Much Politeness Is Too Much?
paras: Imagine you need directions in a new city. In Oslo, Where is the station? is a perfectly normal question. Norwegians are famously straightforward: they get to the point, and a long, careful question can even sound strange to them, as if you were hiding something.

Ask the same thing in London and it may come across as a little blunt. A British speaker is more likely to say Sorry, could you tell me where the station is? or even I was just wondering if you knew where the station was. The British tend to hedge, especially when they feel they are imposing on somebody.

Americans usually sit somewhere in the middle. They are friendly and quick: Hi! Do you know where the station is? is courteous enough almost everywhere in the United States. Too much hedging can even sound awkward, as if the question were a bigger favor than it is.

Notice what happens to the grammar as the question becomes more polite. Where is the station? becomes Could you tell me where the station is? The question moves to the front, and the second half goes back to the normal order of a statement. So the polite version is not only longer. It is built differently. And the skill at this level is not knowing one polite form, but choosing the right one for the person in front of you.

reading.prompt: Read once, quickly. Which title fits the whole text best?
choices: Why the British are more polite than Norwegians
How to find the station in three European cities
The right amount of politeness depends on who you ask, and polite questions have their own word order

items: In Oslo, Where is the station? sounds rude.
The text says it is a perfectly normal question there. Norwegians are straightforward.
A British speaker often adds words like sorry or I was just wondering.
The British tend to hedge, especially when they feel they are imposing.
Americans usually hedge more than the British.
They sit in the middle. Too much hedging can even sound awkward in the United States.
In a polite question, the second half has the word order of a statement.
Could you tell me where the station IS — not where is the station.
The text says there is one correct polite form for every situation.
The skill is choosing the right form for the person in front of you.
